stances.claim: The Supreme Court — not Malacañang — will ultimately rule on Arroyo's fate; the Palace can investigate, prosecute, cite precedents, and huff, but the SC can alter jurisprudence or create exceptions, and its might rests entirely on its being right — a judgment that will come from the people and from history.

stances.claim: The Arroyo case is uniquely politically charged: De Lima's defiance of the SC TRO nearly precipitated a constitutional crisis, and if the SC issues another TRO allowing Arroyo to fly, the question is whether the Palace will comply or 'do another Leila' — testing the rule of law at its most fundamental institutional level.

notable_anecdotes: The DOJ Circular 41 irony: the very watch-list order authority that De Lima used to block GMA was a circular issued during GMA's own administration — deployed as the ultimate irony of executive accountability, where a former president's own bureaucratic instrument is used to restrain her.

Judge Mupas determining probable cause in just 4 hours — the government's defense (speed was necessary because Arroyo was about to fly) vs the defense's challenge (inconceivable that voluminous records could be reviewed in 4 hours) — CJ presents both sides without endorsing either, modeling his 'each case is unique' principle.

The 'do another Leila' formulation — using De Lima's defiance of the SC TRO as the institutional precedent that the Palace might repeat — reducing a complex constitutional crisis scenario to a vivid verb phrase that encapsulates the rule-of-law stakes of the entire dispute.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban maps the legal battle over former President Arroyo's right to travel against the Aquino administration's accountability goal. Justice Secretary De Lima issued a watch-list order (ironic note: under DOJ Circular 41 issued during GMA's own administration) and physically blocked Arroyo at the airport despite the SC's TRO, nearly precipitating a constitutional crisis. The Comelec's electoral sabotage case in Pasay RTC (Judge Mupas, arrest warrant issued) is now challenged on three fronts: (1) the DOJ-Comelec joint preliminary investigation compromised Comelec's constitutional independence; the government counters that RA 9369 gives DOJ concurrent jurisdiction; (2) the RTC lacks jurisdiction over a high official, which belongs to the Sandiganbayan; the government counters that the Omnibus Election Code gives the RTC exclusive jurisdiction over election offenses; (3) Judge Mupas could not have personally determined probable cause in only 4 hours; the government counters that speed was essential since Arroyo was about to fly. CJ notes the government is also speeding up other cases as backup travel bars. He frames the ultimate question as: will the SC rule correctly, and if it issues a TRO allowing Arroyo to fly, will the Palace comply or 'do another Leila'? He closes with the institutional reminder that 'the might of the Supreme Court rests on its being right -- a judgment that will come from our people and from history.'
